title: Waves, Light and Information
bigQuestion: How can a wave, a beam of light or a pattern of beats carry something from one place to another?

story.title: A Message Across the Gym
story.kicker: Two friends, one flashlight, and a code that turns blinks into words.
paragraphs: The gym at Jamal's school in Illinois was big and loud. On rainy days the whole class had indoor recess there. Jamal's best friend Rosa was at the far end, and yelling did no good. So Jamal brought a flashlight from home. He had learned something over the weekend, and he wanted to try it.

He pointed the flashlight at the wall near Rosa and clicked it: short, short, short. Then three long flashes. Then three short ones again. Rosa stared. Then she grinned. She had learned the same thing. Short-short-short, long-long-long, short-short-short is the most famous emergency signal in the world: SOS.

Rosa did not have a flashlight, so she used her hands. She thumped the wooden bleacher: three quick taps, three slow taps, three quick taps. Jamal felt it before he heard it, a buzz through the wood. Sound had crossed the gym as a wave, just as the light had. Neither the light nor the sound was a thing you could hold. Each was a pattern, moving.

By the end of recess they had worked out signals for "yes," "no," and "meet me at the door." Nothing traveled across the gym except light and sound. No paper, no phone, no runner. Yet the message got through. That is what waves can do. They carry patterns, and patterns can carry meaning.
story.think: Jamal's flashlight blinks and Rosa's taps carried the same message. What did the two signals have in common, and what was different?

lessons.title: Waves in a Rope and a Pond
lessons.mainIdea: A wave is a repeating pattern of motion that moves energy from place to place while the material itself stays put.
reading: Tie one end of a jump rope to a doorknob. Pull it tight and snap your wrist up and down. A bump races along the rope to the door. The rope did not travel. Each piece of rope moved up and down, then came back. The bump is a *wave*. A wave is a pattern that moves through something.

Drop a pebble in a still pond. Rings spread outward. Now watch a leaf floating nearby. As the rings pass, the leaf bobs up and down. It does not race away with the rings. Water waves move the water up and down, and the pattern rolls on. The water stays close to where it was.

What travels with the wave is *energy*. Energy is the ability to make things move or change. A big wave on Lake Michigan can toss a boat and push sand up the beach. The water in that wave did not come all the way across the lake. The energy in the wave did.

words.d: a repeating pattern of motion that moves through water, air, a rope or another material
the ability to make things move or change

look.title: The Leaf on the Pond
look.text: A student tosses a pebble into a pond and watches a leaf floating two meters away. Rings spread out from the splash. When they reach the leaf, it rises, dips, rises, dips, and then sits still again. The leaf ends up almost exactly where it started.
look.prompt: If the water itself is not traveling outward, what is? How do you know something reached the leaf?

check.q: A bump travels down a jump rope. What does the rope itself do?
choices: Each part moves up and down and returns
The rope slides toward the door
check.why: The pattern moves along the rope, but each piece of rope only moves up and down in place.

check.q: What does a wave carry from place to place?
check.why: The material stays close to where it was. The energy travels with the wave pattern.

check.q: Rings from a pebble pass a floating leaf. What happens to the leaf?
choices: It races away with the rings
It bobs up and down and stays near its spot
It is pushed back toward the splash
check.why: Water waves move the water up and down. The leaf rides those bobs but does not travel with the rings.

lessons.title: Amplitude and Wavelength
lessons.mainIdea: Amplitude is how tall a wave is, and wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next; both can be measured and drawn.
reading: Waves come in sizes. Snap the jump rope gently and a small bump travels. Snap it hard and a tall bump travels. The height of the wave above its resting line is its *amplitude*. Bigger amplitude means more energy. Ocean waves with a big amplitude are the ones that knock you over.

Now shake the rope up and down over and over. You see a chain of bumps and dips. The top of each bump is a *crest*. The distance from one crest to the next crest is the *wavelength*. Shake faster and the crests crowd together, so the wavelength gets shorter. Shake slower and it stretches out.

You can describe any wave with these two measurements. Scientists draw a wave as a wavy line. Then they label the amplitude and the wavelength. This site has a wave bench. There you can change each one and watch what happens. Try making a wave that is tall and long. Then make one that is short and small.

words.d: the height of a wave above its resting line; a measure of its energy
the highest point of a wave
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next crest

look.title: Two Drawings of Waves
look.text: Drawing A shows a wavy line with tall bumps spaced far apart. Drawing B shows a wavy line with short bumps packed close together. Both lines are the same length across the page. A student says Drawing B must carry more energy because it has more bumps.
look.prompt: Which drawing has the bigger amplitude? Which has the longer wavelength? Is the student right about energy?

check.q: What is the amplitude of a wave?
choices: Its height above the resting line
check.why: Amplitude is the height of the wave. Bigger amplitude means more energy.

check.q: You shake a rope faster. What happens to the wavelength?
check.why: Shaking faster makes crests come closer together, so the distance between them shrinks.

check.q: Which wave probably carries the most energy?
check.why: Amplitude shows energy. A tall wave has a big amplitude, so it carries more energy.

lessons.title: Waves Move Things
lessons.mainIdea: Because waves carry energy, they can make objects move, from a bobbing toy boat to a fluttering sheet of paper.
reading: Waves do work. Put a toy boat in a bathtub and slap the water at the other end. The boat rocks. Slap harder, with a bigger amplitude, and it rocks more. The energy of your slap traveled through the water and reached the boat. That is how waves make objects move.

*Sound* is a wave too. It travels through air as a pattern of pushes, a *vibration* that spreads out. Stand next to a big drum when someone strikes it. You feel the thump in your chest. Hold a sheet of paper near a loud speaker and it flutters. The air carried a wave to the paper and made it move.

Big waves can do big things. Storm waves on Lake Michigan have thrown chunks of ice and stones onto the Chicago lakefront. Earthquake waves shake the ground and can crack roads. Engineers who build harbors and bridges have to plan for the energy a wave brings.

words.d: a wave of pushes that travels through air, water or solids and that we can hear
a quick back-and-forth shaking

look.title: Speed of Sound in Different Materials
look.prompt: Rosa's taps reached Jamal through the wooden bleacher before he heard them through the air. What does this table suggest about why?

check.q: Why does a toy boat rock more when you slap the water harder?
check.why: A harder slap makes a wave with bigger amplitude, and bigger amplitude means more energy reaches the boat.

check.q: A sheet of paper flutters near a loud speaker. What moved it?
choices: A sound wave in the air
check.why: Sound is a wave of pushes in the air. The pushes reached the paper and made it move.

check.q: According to the table, in which material does sound travel fastest?
check.why: Sound travels at about 5,960 meters per second in steel, far faster than in water or air.

lessons.title: Light Bounces Into Your Eyes
lessons.mainIdea: We see an object because light from a source bounces off it and enters our eyes; with no light, we see nothing.
reading: Sit in a closet with the door shut and the light off. Wait. No matter how long you wait, you cannot see the shelf in front of you. Your eyes work fine. There is just no light. Now open the door a crack. Light slips in, hits the shelf, and *reflects* toward your eyes. Now you can see it.

To reflect means to bounce off. Light leaves a *source* like the sun, a lamp or a flashlight. It travels in straight lines until it hits something. Some of it bounces off. If the bounced light reaches your eyes, you see the object. The eye does not send anything out. It only catches light coming in.

For a long time many people believed the opposite. They thought the eyes sent out beams that felt objects. About a thousand years ago a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham argued from experiments that this could not be true. Looking at the sun hurts because light is coming in, not going out.

words.d: to bounce off a surface, as light bounces off objects
something that gives off light, like the sun or a lamp

look.title: A Book About Sight
look.text: Around the year 1020, in his Book of Optics, Ibn al-Haytham argued that we see because light travels from a lit object into the eye, not because the eye sends out rays. He pointed out that looking at a very bright light hurts the eye and leaves a spot in your vision afterward. That only makes sense if something is entering the eye.
look.cite: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), Book of Optics, about 1020 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Ibn al-Haytham used a painful experience as evidence. What would the old 'eye beam' idea predict instead, and why does it fail?

check.q: Why can't you see a shelf in a completely dark closet?
choices: No light is bouncing off the shelf into your eyes
The shelf is invisible in the dark
Your eyes need time to send out beams
check.why: Seeing needs light. With no source, no light reflects off the shelf, so nothing reaches your eyes.

check.q: Which of these is a light source?
check.why: A flashlight makes its own light. The moon, a mirror and a wall only reflect light from somewhere else.

check.q: What did Ibn al-Haytham argue about how we see?
choices: Eyes send out beams that touch objects
Light enters the eye from lit objects
check.why: He argued from experiments that light travels from objects into the eye, not the other way around.

lessons.title: Mirrors and Shadows
lessons.mainIdea: Light travels in straight lines, which is why mirrors show clear reflections and objects cast shadows.
reading: Shine a flashlight through a dusty room. The beam is a straight bar of light. Light does not bend around corners on its own. That is why you cannot see around a corner, and why a wall blocks a lamp. When an object blocks light, a dark patch forms behind it. That patch is a *shadow*.

A *mirror* is a very smooth, shiny surface. Light bounces off it at the same angle it came in, like a ball off a wall. Because the bounce is so neat, the light forms a clear picture. A rough surface, like paper, scatters light in every direction. You can see paper, but you cannot see yourself in it.

You can send a beam around a corner with mirrors. Point a flashlight at a mirror at the right angle and the beam turns. Add a second mirror and it turns again. A periscope uses two mirrors so a person in a submarine can see above the water. Light only goes straight, but mirrors can redirect it.

words.d: a dark patch behind an object that blocks light
a very smooth, shiny surface that reflects light in a neat, clear way

look.title: Around the Corner
look.text: A student builds a periscope from a tall cardboard tube. She fits a small mirror at the top, tilted, and another at the bottom, tilted the other way. Looking into the bottom hole, she can see over a fence that is taller than she is.
look.prompt: Trace the path of light from the top of the fence to her eye. How many times does it bounce, and why does the trick work?

check.q: Why does a wall block the light from a lamp?
choices: Light cannot bend around the wall
Light is too slow to reach the other side
The lamp is not bright enough
check.why: Light travels in straight lines. It cannot curve around the wall, so a shadow forms behind it.

check.q: Why can you see yourself in a mirror but not in a sheet of paper?
choices: Paper does not reflect any light
A mirror is smooth, so light bounces in a neat pattern
A mirror makes its own light
check.why: A smooth mirror bounces light at the same angle it came in, forming a clear picture. Paper scatters light everywhere.

check.q: A periscope uses two mirrors. What do the mirrors do to the light?
check.why: Light goes straight between bounces. Each mirror turns the beam, so two mirrors let it go up and over.

lessons.title: Light Bends in Water
lessons.mainIdea: When light passes from air into water or glass, it slows and bends; that is why a straw looks broken and a lens can focus light.
reading: Put a straw in a glass of water and look from the side. The straw looks broken at the water line. It is not. Light from the underwater part of the straw bends as it leaves the water and enters the air. Your eye follows the bent light and sees the straw in the wrong place. This bending is called *refraction*.

Light bends because it slows down when it enters water or glass. In water, light moves at about three-quarters of its speed in air. The change in speed turns the beam. Think of a shopping cart. One wheel rolls onto grass while the other stays on the sidewalk. The cart swings toward the grass. Light does the same at the edge of the water.

A *lens* is a curved piece of glass or plastic that uses refraction on purpose. A lens that bulges in the middle bends light toward a point. That is how a magnifying glass makes small things look big. It is also how the microscope and the telescope on this site work. Your own eye has a lens, too.

words.d: the bending of light when it passes from one material into another
a curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light on purpose

look.title: How Fast Light Travels
look.prompt: Light bends more when its speed changes more. Which material would bend a beam of light the most as it enters from air?

check.q: Why does a straw in water look broken?
choices: Light bends as it leaves the water
check.why: Refraction bends the light from the underwater part, so your eye sees that part in the wrong place.

check.q: What happens to light when it enters water from air?
check.why: Light travels slower in water than in air. The change in speed makes the beam turn.

check.q: What does a magnifying glass do to light?
choices: Blocks it to make a shadow
check.why: A lens that bulges in the middle refracts light toward a point, which makes small things look big.

lessons.title: Dots, Dashes and Blinks
lessons.mainIdea: A code turns letters into a pattern of short and long signals, so a flashlight or a wire can carry words.
reading: A *code* is an agreement about what patterns mean. In the 1830s and 1840s, Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail built a code out of short and long electric pulses. A short pulse is a dot. A long one is a dash. The letter S is three dots. The letter O is three dashes. Together, they spell the emergency call SOS.

In 1844, Morse sent the first public message over a wire from Washington to Baltimore. The pulses arrived almost at once. Before that, a letter took days. Within a few years, telegraph wires reached Chicago, and news could cross Illinois in minutes. A *signal* is any pattern sent to carry a message.

Morse code works with anything that can be on or off. A flashlight can blink it. A whistle can chirp it. Ships still use signal lamps to flash it between decks. The wave that carries it does not matter, as long as the sender and the receiver agree on the code.

words.d: an agreement about what each pattern of signals means
a pattern sent from one place to another to carry a message

look.title: The First Public Telegraph Message
look.cite: Samuel F. B. Morse, telegraph message sent from Washington to Baltimore, May 24, 1844
look.prompt: These four words crossed about 40 miles of wire in an instant as electric pulses. What had to be true at both ends of the wire for the message to be read?

check.q: In Morse code, what is the letter S?
check.why: S is three short signals, or dots. O is three long signals, or dashes.

check.q: Why can a flashlight send Morse code?
choices: Because light is faster than electricity
Because it can be turned on and off in a pattern
Because light is a kind of wire
check.why: Morse code needs only short and long signals. A flashlight can blink short and long.

check.q: What must be true for a coded message to work?
choices: The signal must be very loud
Sender and receiver must agree on the code
The wire must be made of copper
check.why: A code is an agreement. If the receiver does not know the code, the pattern is just noise.

lessons.title: Drum Talk
lessons.mainIdea: Beats on a drum can carry a message across a distance because people agree on what each pattern means.
reading: Long before wires, people sent messages with sound. In parts of West Africa, drummers used special drums to send news from village to village. A trained listener far away could hear the *rhythm* and understand it. Rhythm is a *pattern* of beats and pauses in time. The sound wave carried the pattern through the air.

A drum message has parts you can change. You can hit hard or soft, which changes the amplitude of the sound wave. You can hit fast or slow. You can leave long gaps or short ones. Each choice is a piece of the pattern. Put the pieces together and you have a signal.

Try it with a partner and the drum bench on this site, or a desk and your hands. Agree on three patterns: one for yes, one for no, one for help. Then turn your backs and send messages. If the patterns are too alike, mistakes happen. Good codes use patterns that are easy to tell apart.

words.d: a pattern of beats and pauses in time
something that repeats or follows a rule you can recognize

look.title: Two Codes
look.text: Team A decides that 'yes' is two taps and 'no' is three taps. Team B decides that 'yes' is two quick taps and 'no' is one slow, heavy thump. Across a noisy room, Team A keeps getting messages wrong. Team B almost never does.
look.prompt: Why does Team B's code work better in a noisy room? What makes two patterns easy to tell apart?

check.q: What carries a drum message from one village to another?
choices: A sound wave through the air
check.why: The drum makes a sound wave. The wave travels through the air and carries the rhythm.

check.q: Hitting the drum harder changes which part of the sound wave?
check.why: A harder hit makes a louder sound, which means a sound wave with bigger amplitude.

check.q: Why should code patterns be very different from each other?
choices: So they take longer to send
So the receiver does not mix them up
check.why: Patterns that are too alike are easy to confuse, especially when there is noise.

lessons.title: Ones and Zeros
lessons.mainIdea: Computers send pictures, sounds and words as long strings of just two signals, on and off, called binary.
reading: A phone or a computer sends everything as *binary*. Binary uses only two signals, written as 1 and 0. A 1 can be a flash of light, a pulse of electricity or a burst of radio. A 0 is a gap. Each 1 or 0 is called a *bit*. Bits are the smallest pieces of a *digital* message.

How can two signals say anything? By making patterns. With one bit you can make two patterns: 1 or 0. With two bits you get four: 00, 01, 10, 11. Every extra bit doubles the count. Eight bits make 256 patterns, enough for every letter, number and mark on a keyboard. The letter A, for example, is 01000001.

Every photo you have ever sent was a long string of bits. Some traveled as flashes of light down a glass thread thinner than a hair. Some traveled as radio waves from a Wi-Fi router. Some ran as electric pulses along copper wires. Different waves, same code: on and off, over and over, very fast.

words.d: a code that uses only two signals, written as 1 and 0
a single 1 or 0, the smallest piece of a digital message
made of separate on-or-off signals rather than a smooth, changing one

look.title: How Many Patterns Bits Can Make
look.cite: counting rule: each added bit doubles the number of patterns
look.prompt: Find the rule in the numbers. How many patterns could 5 bits make? Why are 8 bits enough for every key on a keyboard?

check.q: How many different signals does binary use?
check.why: Binary uses only two signals, 1 and 0, which can be on and off.

check.q: With 3 bits, how many patterns can you make?
check.why: Each added bit doubles the count: 2, then 4, then 8.

check.q: Which wave can carry binary?
choices: Any of these, as long as it can be on or off
check.why: Binary needs only an on-and-off signal. Light, radio and electric pulses can all do that.

lessons.title: Clean Signals Over Long Distances
lessons.mainIdea: Digital signals of on and off can be copied and sent again without mistakes, which is why they carry messages so far.
reading: Every wave gets weaker as it travels. Shout across a field and your voice fades. Along the way, other sounds mix in. Scientists call this unwanted mix *noise*. A soft, smooth signal like a voice is hard to fix once noise gets in. You cannot tell which wobbles were the message.

A digital signal is different. The *receiver* only has to decide one thing: was that on or off? Even a weak, fuzzy flash is clearly not a gap. So a receiver can read the bits, make a fresh, strong copy, and send it on. Do this every few miles and the message crosses an ocean as clean as it started.

That is why a text from Chicago reaches a friend in another country without a single wrong letter. It is also why Jamal's flashlight worked across a noisy gym. Rosa never had to hear his voice. She only had to see light or no light. Simple patterns are hard to break.

words.d: unwanted signals that mix into a message and make it harder to read
the person or machine that takes in a signal and reads it

look.title: The Fading Whisper
look.text: Twenty students stand in a line. The first whispers a sentence to the next, and so on. By the end, the sentence is nonsense. Then they try again with a rule: only tap once for yes or twice for no. This time the last student gets every answer right, even with a loud fan running.
look.prompt: Why did the tapping game survive the line and the fan when the whisper did not? How is this like a digital signal?

check.q: What is noise, in this lesson?
choices: Unwanted signals mixed into a message
check.why: Noise is anything that gets mixed into a signal and makes the real message harder to read.

check.q: Why can a weak digital signal still be read correctly?
choices: The receiver only has to tell on from off
check.why: Even a fuzzy flash is clearly on, not off. That simple choice makes bits easy to read and copy.

check.q: Why did the flashlight message work in a noisy gym?
choices: The signal was a simple on-or-off pattern
check.why: Rosa only needed to see light or no light. Noise in the gym could not change that pattern.

review.q: A wave passes a floating duck. The duck:
choices: Bobs up and down and stays near its spot
review.why: Water waves move water up and down. The wave pattern travels on, but the duck stays close to where it was.

choices: The distance from one crest to the next
review.why: Wavelength is the distance between neighboring crests. Amplitude is the height.

review.q: You feel a drum thump in your chest. What reached you?
review.why: Sound is a wave of pushes through the air. Its energy can move your chest and a sheet of paper.

review.q: You see a red apple because:
choices: Your eyes send beams to the apple
The apple makes its own light
Red is a kind of sound
Light bounces off the apple into your eyes
review.why: Light from a source reflects off the apple. Some of that light enters your eyes.

review.q: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent because:
choices: Light bends when it moves from water to air
The water pushes on the pencil
Your eyes get confused by wet things
review.why: Refraction bends the light leaving the water, so your eye sees the underwater part in the wrong place.

choices: Three dashes, three dots, three dashes
Three dots, three dashes, three dots
review.why: S is three dots and O is three dashes, so SOS is dot-dot-dot, dash-dash-dash, dot-dot-dot.

review.q: Which best describes a digital signal?
choices: A message that must be shouted
A pattern made of on-and-off signals
review.why: Digital signals use separate on-or-off pieces, called bits, instead of a smooth changing wave.

review.q: Why can digital messages travel across an ocean without errors?
choices: The message is sent only once
Receivers copy the bits fresh and send them on
review.why: A receiver only decides on or off, then makes a strong new copy. Noise cannot pile up.
